summary: Suggests a straightforward convention for describing SNMP-based agents, so that what each agent supports can be written down consistently. It is informational and not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Every gadget needs a clear label saying what it can do. This paper suggests a standard way to write that label for network monitoring programs.

questions: how to describe an snmp agent
what does the variation clause do in snmp
subtitle: A macro that lets an SNMP agent publish exactly which MIB groups it supports and how it deviates from them.

tldr.problem: An SNMP agent may implement only some MIB groups, or implement some objects with restricted syntax or access, and there was no concise way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1303 defines the MODULE-CONFORMANCE macro, whose value is the agent's sysObjectID. It lists supported MIB modules and groups, plus per-object variations.
tldr.outcome: Management station implementors can keep a database of these descriptions and tune their applications to each agent. The memo is Informational and is not a protocol.

today: RFC 1303 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC states that security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: The Management Framework and Its Objects
sections.content:
The Internet-standard Network Management Framework has three components: RFC 1155 (the SMI, which describes and names objects) with RFC 1212 (a more concise description mechanism), RFC 1213 (MIB-II, the core set of managed objects) and RFC 1157 (SNMP, the protocol for network access to managed objects).

Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the MIB. Each object has at minimum a name, a syntax, an access-level and an implementation-status. The name is an object identifier. The syntax is written in ASN.1. The access-level says whether it makes protocol sense to read or write the object, independent of any administrative policy. The status says whether the object is mandatory, optional, obsolete or deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: A network device keeps a big list of facts about itself. Each fact has a name, a type, a rule for who may read or change it, and a note on whether it is required.

sections.title: Why Describe Agents
sections.content:
A MIB module is divided into groups. An agent that claims a group must implement every object in it, but it may implement only a subset of the groups. Some object definitions also leave details to the implementor.

The memo defines the MODULE-CONFORMANCE macro so an implementor can state the precise level of support and bind it to the agent's sysObjectID. A management station can then keep a database of these descriptions. On meeting an agent it reads the sysObjectID, looks it up and, if an entry exists, optimizes its behavior.

The binding to sysObjectID may not be enough when an agent learns its objects dynamically, for example an agent supporting SMUX peers. In that case, additional MIB objects must name further invocations of the macro. The RFC's example is that each instance of smuxPidentity indicates another invocation being supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every gadget does everything. A short description of what each one can do lets the control program skip things that will not work.

sections.title: The MODULE-CONFORMANCE Macro
sections.content:
The macro is defined in ASN.1 macro notation in a module called RFC-1303, which imports ObjectName and ObjectSyntax from RFC 1155 and DisplayString from RFC 1213. Its value is the agent's sysObjectID.

The body starts with LAST-UPDATED, PRODUCT-RELEASE and DESCRIPTION. Then come zero or more SUPPORTS modules. Each names a MIB module, optionally with its object identifier, and an INCLUDES list of groups. Each module may carry VARIATION entries, which can have SYNTAX, WRITE-SYNTAX, ACCESS, CREATION-REQUIRES and DEFVAL parts and must have a DESCRIPTION.

The RFC notes that expanding the macro conceptually happens during implementation, not at run-time.
sections.plainLanguage: The macro is a fill-in form with fixed boxes: who made it, what it is, which feature sets it has, and where it differs from the standard.

sections.title: What Each Clause Means
sections.content:
LAST-UPDATED holds the date and time the definition was last edited. PRODUCT-RELEASE describes the product release containing the agent. DESCRIPTION describes the agent. All three must be present. SUPPORTS need not be present, but when it is used, INCLUDES must be given for each use.

A VARIATION names an object the agent implements in a refined way. SYNTAX refines the syntax, and when WRITE-SYNTAX is also present, SYNTAX applies only to reads. ACCESS may be read-only, read-write, write-only or not-accessible. CREATION-REQUIRES names the columnar objects that a SNMP Set must assign before the agent will create a new row. It must not appear unless the object is a conceptual row, and its absence means the agent does not support creating rows through SNMP. DEFVAL gives a refined default value.

Syntax refinements have limits: the primitive or application type must not change, objects of type OBJECT IDENTIFIER, IpAddress, Counter or TimeTicks cannot be refined, and an object with a specific set of named values cannot gain more values.
sections.plainLanguage: Some boxes on the form are required and some are optional. The rules also say you may narrow what a feature does, but never widen it.

sections.title: The 4BSD/ISODE Example
sections.content:
The RFC documents the 4BSD/ISODE "Secure" SNMP agent. It supports four MIB modules: the SNMP Party MIB groups partyPublic and partyPrivate, all MIB-II groups except egp, three groups from a UNIX-MIB, and two from an EVAL-MIB.

For MIB-II it lists variations. Some objects, such as ipInAddrErrors and tcpInErrs, are not available. Others, such as ifAdminStatus and ipDefaultTTL, have restricted syntax. tcpConnState is read-only. For ipRouteType and ipNetToMediaType the readable values differ from the writable values. Creating a new row in atTable, ipRouteTable or ipNetToMediaTable requires setting atPhysAddress, ipRouteNextHop or ipNetToMediaPhysAddress respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a label for one real program. It says which groups of features work fully, which are missing, and which can be read but not changed.
